Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify common sites and correlating muscle attachments for pelvic avulsion fractures.
Describe the first-line treatment approach for pelvic avulsion fractures.
Explain the classification of pediatric hip fractures (Delbet classification system).
Determine treatment approaches based on pediatric hip fracture type.
Recognize common complications of pediatric hip fractures.
Explain the classification of pediatric pelvis fractures.
Recognize the importance of concomitant injuries observed in pediatric patients with a pelvic
fracture.
Review treatment approaches for pediatric pelvis fractures.
Pelvic Avulsion Fractures




NOTES

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Typically occur in adolescent athletes who participate in explosive-type activities, such as
sprinting, jumping, and/or kicking
More common in males (78%) and mean patient age at the time of injury is 14.6 years1
Common avulsion sites (and the causative muscles) are shown in Table 1.
The most common sites are the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), anterior inferior iliac
spine (AIIS; Figure 1), and ischial tuberosity.2
Table 1 Pelvic Avulsion Fracture Sites and Causative Muscles
Avulsion Site
Causative Muscles
Ischium
 Hamstrings/adductors
Anterior superior iliac spine
 Sartorius
Anterior inferior iliac spine
 Rectus femoris
Iliac crest
 Abdominals
Lesser trochanter
 Iliopsoas
Reproduced from Abousamra O, Kay RM: Pediatric pelvic and lower extremity fractures, in
Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1481-1494.

2/47

Figure 1 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a right anterior inferior iliac spine fracture.
According to the Torode and Zieg classification system, this injury is categorized as a type I
pediatric pelvic fracture. (Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck, MD, Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD,
Washington, DC; and Wendy Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati, OH.)
Anatomy
These injuries consist of a fracture through the apophyseal growth plate.
Classification
These fractures are included in the Torode and Zieg classification as type I pediatric pelvic
fractures.3
Assessing the amount of displacement also is important because displacement greater than 1
to 3 cm increases the risk of nonunion.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Determine the activity or action being performed at the time the injury occurred.
Often occurs during sporting events
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
3/47

The patient’s age also is important because open growth plates results in an area of weakness
at the origin of the muscle involved at the apophysis, leading to an avulsion fracture. Patients
with closed growth plates tend to sustain avulsion at the musculotendinous junction.

Patient History
These fractures often are observed in adolescent athletes and often occur during
explosive actions. For example, an ASIS avulsion injury can occur as a soccer player
sends a crossing pass. Typically, sudden pain and inability to participate occurs,
occasionally with inability to ambulate. The injury occurs through the involved
apophyseal growth plate.
Physical Examination
Symptoms may be similar to those of muscle strain or apophysitis.
Assess gait.
Assess for areas of tenderness to palpation.
Assess for pain with resisted movements because this pain may indicate which muscle the
avulsion fracture involves.
Assess for pain with passive stretching (typically hyperextension of the joint) of the affected
muscle.

Physical Examination
The physical examination typically reveals tenderness at the site of avulsion injury and
pain with active motion of the involved muscle. For example, hip flexion will be painful in
a patient with an ASIS avulsion injury.
Neurovascular Examination
A complete bilateral lower extremity neurovascular examination should be performed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
4/47


Neurovascular Examination
Surgeons should evaluate for deficits that may be secondary to sciatic nerve and lateral
femoral cutaneous nerve damage because these nerves may be affected by ischial
tuberosity and ASIS avulsions, respectively.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP pelvis radiograph
Judet views or a false-profile lateral view may be helpful to assess for subtle displacement of
ASIS and AIIS fractures. In addition, the contralateral side can be used for comparison.
Computed Tomography/Magnetic Resonance Imaging
In patients in whom radiographs are not diagnostic, advanced imaging studies, such as CT or
MRI, can be obtained; however, the need for these modalities to diagnose an avulsion fracture
is uncommon.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Local measures, including rest, ice, protected–weight bearing, and anti-inflammatory
medications for 2 to 3 weeks, are followed by gradual resumption of activities.
A five-step protocol to manage all pelvic and trochanteric avulsion fractures was published
by Metzmaker and Pappas.4
Stage 1: ice, rest, NSAIDs for 1 week, with non–weight bearing on the affected extremity
Stage 2: gentle passive range of motion and assisted partial–weight bearing from weeks 1
through 3
Stage 3: resistance training beginning in week 4 postinjury
Stage 4: aggressive stretching and sport-specific activity beginning between 1 and 2 months
postinjury
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
5/47

Stage 5: return to sports activity at 2 months postinjury

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is the first line of treatment for almost all patients with a pelvic
avulsion injury. Nonsurgical treatment measures, including rest, ice, temporary
protected–weight bearing, anti-inflammatory medications, and physical therapy may
help patients recover from these injuries. Metzmaker and Pappas4 reported that return
to sports activity often is achieved 2 months postinjury.
Indications
May be the first-line treatment for most pelvic avulsion fractures
Contraindications
Symptomatic nonunion or painful heterotopic ossification
Surgical Management
Surgical management rarely is indicated for these injuries; surgical management may be
considered for symptomatic nonunions.
Indications for surgical management include symptomatic nonunion or heterotopic
ossification that was not successfully managed nonsurgically.
Some studies have suggested that substantial initial displacement also may be best managed
surgically;5-7 however, this is controversial.
Complications
Few long-term sequelae
Nonunion
Symptomatic nonunion is uncommon.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
6/47

Malunion
If substantial displacement is present with AIIS and possibly ASIS avulsion fractures,
femoroacetabular impingement may occur (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction image of a hip demonstrates a right anterior
inferior iliac spine fracture malunion resulting in impingement. (Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck, MD,
Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD, Washington, DC; and Wendy Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati,
OH.)
Hip Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Hip fractures are rare injuries, accounting for less than 1% of all pediatric fractures. Most are
caused by high-energy mechanisms of injury; however, pathologic fractures also result from
low-energy trauma8 (Resource 1).
Anatomy
Osteology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
7/47

The proximal femur consists of the proximal femoral epiphysis, proximal femur physis, and
femoral neck, which are proximal to the greater and lesser trochanters.
The lesser trochanter is the insertion of the iliopsoas.
The greater trochanter is the insertion of much of the hip abductor musculature.
Vascular Anatomy
Blood supply to the femoral head directly from the metaphysis is present until approximately
age 4 years, after which lateral epiphyseal vessels become the primary blood supply to the
epiphysis. These vessels are branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery.9
Classification
The Delbet classification system is used for proximal femur fractures (Figure 3).
The Delbet classification uses the fracture location to classify femoral neck fractures:
Type I: transphyseal
Type II: transcervical
Type III: cervicotrochanteric
Type IV, intertrochanteric
Subtrochanteric femur fractures are not included in the Delbet classification system.
Figure 3 Illustrations show the Delbet classification of pediatric hip fractures. Type I fractures are
physeal. Type II fractures are transcervical. Type III fractures are cervicotrochanteric. Type IV
fractures are intertrochanteric. (Reproduced with permission from Hughes LO, Beaty JH:
Fractures of the head and neck of the femur in children. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1994;76[2]:283-292.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
8/47


Classification
The Delbet classification system helps surgeons determine the best management
approach, including fixation options, and aids in preoperative discussions with the
patient’s family with regard to the risk of complications, such as osteonecrosis.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The patient history should include patient age, mechanism of injury, and relevant medical
history.
Rule out child abuse.
Physical Examination
Evaluation for deformity of the affected extremity and evaluation of neurovascular status of
the extremity are key.
In addition, a secondary survey evaluating for other injuries is important. A hip fracture may
distract from recognition of other injuries sustained during a high-energy event.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
An AP pelvis radiograph should be obtained to allow for contralateral hip comparison.
The lateral radiograph can be a frog-lateral or cross-table lateral view. A cross-table lateral
view should be considered to avoid additional discomfort for the patient and the potential for
additional displacement.
With displaced femoral neck fractures, assessing the exact location and classification of the
fracture may be difficult. In these cases, an AP radiograph with gentle traction and internal
rotation of the leg is helpful to better assess the injury pattern.
Computed Tomography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
9/47

CT may be considered to evaluate nondisplaced fractures or stress fractures and can be
performed if the fracture pattern is uncertain to allow for preoperative planning.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is useful in identifying minimally displaced fractures, pathologic fractures, and stress
fractures.
Preferred imaging modality in assessing for nondisplaced or stress fractures
Also can be performed if osteonecrosis is a concern postinjury
Differential Diagnosis
Infection
Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is infrequently indicated because of the increased risks of coxa vara
and nonunion with closed management.
Indications 
In patients younger than 1 year who have a nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture,
treatment can be via a Pavlik harness or an abduction orthosis.
In patients younger than 5 years, nondisplaced Delbet type II and type III fractures can be
managed via hip spica cast immobilization.
Patients with a nondisplaced pathologic fracture should undergo simultaneous treatment of
the associated lesion, especially before displacement. The surgeon must consider the risks and
advantages of transphyseal fixation.
Contraindications
Displaced fractures10
Delbet type I fracture in child older than 2 years
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
10/47

Surgical Management
Early surgical management is recommended.11,12
Anatomic reduction12 and stable fixation are key to successful management.11,13
If feasible, gentle, closed reduction and internal fixation is preferred.
If residual displacement remains, open reduction should be performed.14
Can be performed via anterior, anterolateral, or surgical hip dislocation approaches
Fixation
Fixation is performed with the use of Kirschner wires or cannulated screws for Delbet type I
fractures; cannulated screws for type II and type III fractures (some surgeons opt to use
physeal-friendly screw options, which are available for certain pediatric proximal femoral
locking plates); and a pediatric hip screw, dynamic hip screw, or proximal femur locking plate
for type IV fractures.
Stability of fixation is paramount to reduce the risk of nonunion or malunion. Fixation should
extend across the physis if necessary for stability.
Multiple fixation constructs are available based on the fracture pattern and the size of the
patient. If uncertainty exists with regard to the ability of a patient to comply with
postoperative weight-bearing restrictions, a hip spica cast should be applied at the end of the
procedure.
Indications
Displaced fractures10 (Resource 2)
Patient older than 5 years
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
An understanding of the fracture pattern is important to determine appropriate fixation.
Fluoroscopy will be necessary, and the fluoroscopy unit typically is positioned on the opposite
side of the table from the surgeon.
Patient Positioning
Depends on anticipated approach if open reduction will be performed
Radiolucent table: flat top or fracture table
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
11/47

Surgical Approaches
If open reduction is necessary, options include anterior, anterolateral, and surgical hip
dislocation approaches.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Type I
Reduction can be attempted via hip extension, abduction, and internal rotation. Knee flexion
also may assist in the maneuver.
In small children, 2-mm Kirschner wires can be used for fixation.
In larger children, multiple cannulated screws crossing the physis can be used. Care must be
taken to avoid articular penetration of the screws (Figures 4 and 5).
Figure 4 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a Delbet type I hip fracture. (Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck,
MD, Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD, Washington, DC; and Wendy Ramalingam, MD,
Cincinnati, OH.)
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 5 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates surgical fixation of a Delbet type I hip fracture.
(Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck, MD, Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD, Washington, DC; and
Wendy Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati, OH.)
Type II
Internal fixation with the use of cannulated screws typically results in stability (Figures 6 and
7).
Stable fixation is key. Crossing the physis may be unavoidable.
The literature supports the use of a proximal femoral locking plate, some of which offer
nonthreaded tipped screws, which are more physeal-friendly; however, risks of poor
compression and/or loss of fixation continue to be studied15 (Figure 8; Video 1).

Type III
Internal fixation with the use of cannulated screws
Also may consider a compression hip screw or locking plate16 (Figures 9 through 11)
Stable fixation is key. With this more distal fracture pattern, crossing the physis with implants
often is avoidable, thereby decreasing the risk of growth disturbance.

Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati, OH.)

Figure 11 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates surgical fixation of a Delbet type III hip fracture.

Type IV
Internal fixation with the use of a compression hip screw or a locking plate. Pediatric sizes
are available (Figures 12 and 13).

Insert a derotational wire before drilling and tapping the femoral neck to decrease the risk of
fracture displacement.

(Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck, MD, Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD, Washington, DC; and
Wendy Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati, OH.)

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Several fixation constructs are available depending on the fracture pattern and the size
of the patient. Surgeons should not hesitate to reinforce these constructs with a hip
spica cast postoperatively.
Postoperative Management
Spica cast immobilization should be used if fixation stability is a concern.
If the patient is too young to cross the physis with implants, a spica cast should be used for
postoperative immobilization.
Can be used for 6 weeks postoperatively
Patients should remain non–weight bearing for 6 weeks postoperatively or until evidence of
robust fracture healing is observed on radiographs.
Progressive weight bearing and physical therapy can then be initiated.
Complications
The complication rate after pediatric femoral neck fracture has been reported to be 33%.17
Some risk factors for suboptimal complications in patients with these difficult-to-manage
injuries cannot be modified.18
Complication rates correlate with the Delbet classification system: highest complication rates
associated with Delbet type I fractures, lowest complication rates associated with Delbet type
IV fractures.
Nonunion
Nonunions are much more common after nonsurgical management, particularly in patients
with a Delbet type II or type III fracture (Figure 14).
Nonanatomic reduction or loss of stable fixation may result in nonunion.
Nonunion often can be managed via valgus osteotomy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580

Figure 14 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a nonunion after surgical management of a
femoral neck fracture. (Courtesy of Jeffrey Peck, MD, Washington, DC; Matthew Oetgen, MD,
Washington, DC; and Wendy Ramalingam, MD, Cincinnati, OH.)
Malunion
Coxa vara also is more common after nonsurgical management of type II and type III fractures.
Anatomic reduction and internal fixation have decreased the prevalence of this complication
(Video 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM

Surgeons, San Francisco, CA, February 12-16, 2024.
Other Complications
Osteonecrosis is the most common and severe complication and is related to fracture type,
with a higher risk of osteonecrosis observed in patients with more proximal fractures and
older children19 (Figure 15; Video 3).
Limb-length discrepancy (LLD) is common after hip fractures in young children because the
proximal femur physis accounts for approximately 15% of total leg length.
Physeal arrest may result from type I fractures, violation of the physis with implants, or
osteonecrosis.
After closed reduction of traumatic hip dislocations, imaging studies are necessary to rule out
structural injury to the hip, especially the posterior labrum/chondrolabral junction. MRI has
been shown to be superior to CT in detecting such injuries.


Other Complications
Several complications are associated with pediatric hip fractures, including nonunion,
malunion, osteonecrosis, growth disturbance, and limb-length discrepancy. Timely
management via anatomic reduction and stable fixation is important to decrease the risk
of these complications. The risk of osteonecrosis previously was reported to be as high
as 90% to 100% for type I fractures, 50% for type II fractures, 25% for type III fractures,
and 10% for type IV fractures; however, more recent data demonstrate lower risks of this
complication (38%, 28%, 18%, and 5%, respectively; Resource 3). Osteonecrosis occurs at
a mean of 7.8 months postinjury.20 Femoral head collapse often leads to penetration of
the joint by previously placed hardware, which may result in chondrolysis and
exacerbation of pain.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Urgent reduction (<24 hours) may reduce the risk of osteonecrosis.
Anatomic reduction is vital.
Stable fixation is paramount. (Video 4)

Pediatric Pelvis Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Pelvic fractures are rare in children, with an incidence of 1 per 100,000 children.
These injuries are observed in 5% of all pediatric trauma patients.21
The mean age in population studies is approximately 9 to 11 years.
More common in males than females.22
Pediatric pelvis fractures are associated with lower mortality than adult pelvis fractures.0.
5% versus 17%23
Morbidity and mortality experienced by pediatric patients more likely are secondary to
concomitant visceral and central nervous system injury.
May occur with concomitant acetabular fractures and/or hip dislocations
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The pelvis is formed from three primary ossification centers via endochondral ossification.
Ilium
Pubis
Ischium
Triradiate cartilage forms the acetabulum at the junction of three bones of the pelvis.
Growth and development are closely related to mechanical stimuli/pressure from the
femoral head.
Closure of triradiate cartilage24
Males: mean age, 13.9 years (range, 12.6 to 15.3 years)
Females: mean age, 14.4 years (range, 10.5 to 15.9 years)
Secondary ossification centers throughout the pelvis close at different ages based on location
and sex (Figure 16).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
24/47

Age at secondary ossification center closure varies substantially.
Males: 12.6 to 30.0 years
Females: 10.4 to 30.4 years
The last secondary ossification centers to close are the iliac crest and the symphysis pubis.
Figure 16 Images show osteology of the pelvis. A, AP pelvis radiographs demonstrate normal
pelvic bone anatomy and development at birth (i), age 2 years (ii), age 5 years (iii), and age 15
years (iv). B, Illustration shows the location of ossification centers in the pelvic bone, noting the
time at which they appear and the time at which the physes fuse. Note the Y-shaped triradiate
cartilage at the acetabulum. AIIS = anterior inferior iliac spine. (Reproduced with permission from
DeFrancesco CJ, Sankar WN: Traumatic pelvic fractures in children and adolescents. Semin Pediatr
Surg 2017;26[1]:27-35.)
Pediatric patients are not just little adults.
The bones of pediatric patients have a higher elasticity with thicker periosteum than those in
adults. Pediatric patients also have increased flexibility of the sacroiliac and pubic symphysis
joints.
This difference results in a higher rate of single-bone pelvic fractures in children than in
adults.
Pelvic volume is more shallow in children than adults.
Growth centers are present, which may act as a double-edged sword.
May allow for potential remodeling
May lead to substantial deformity if damaged
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
25/47

May make radiographic diagnosis more difficult for radiologists and orthopaedic surgeons
not trained in pediatrics
Vascular Anatomy
Proximal femur blood supply to the epiphysis is primarily from the posteroinferior and
posterosuperior branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery after age 4 years.9
Pediatric blood vessels tend to undergo vasoconstriction more readily than those in adults.
Along with an increased rate of single-bone pelvic fractures, this factor may be the reason that
substantial morbidity and mortality from hemorrhage is uncommon in pediatric patients.
Neural Anatomy
The lumbosacral plexus, sciatic nerve, femoral nerve, and obturator nerve are at risk from
injury and management of pediatric and adolescent pelvic and acetabular fractures.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Pelvic ring injuries typically result from high-energy mechanisms of injury.25
75% of pediatric pelvic fractures result from motor vehicle collisions or a pedestrian strike.
The mechanism of injury necessitates a comprehensive workup for concomitant injuries.26
Associated injuries
Head trauma
Extremity fractures
Thoracic injury
Visceral injury
Genitourinary injury
Pelvic avulsion fractures typically result from sports activities and low-energy traumatic
mechanisms of injury.
Associated Injuries
Pelvic ring fractures in pediatric patients typically result from high-energy mechanisms of
injury, necessitating careful evaluation for concomitant injuries.
Assessment of a child with a pelvic injury should begin with evaluation of the patient’s airway,
breathing, and circulatory systems.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:39 PM
AAOS | Pelvic and Hip Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000580
26/47

Thorough evaluation of the head, chest, abdomen, and spine are important.
These other injuries are more likely to be life-threatening and should be the primary focus
of initial management.
Evaluation for genitourinary system injury also is vital.
Lower extremity neurologic deficits may result from severe pelvic ring disruptions because of
lumbosacral plexus stretch injury.
Classification
No ideal classification system is available for pediatric pelvic ring injuries.
Varying levels of skeletal maturity lead to different injury patterns based on triradiate
cartilage closure27 (Figure 17).
Figure 17 Bar graph shows the percentage distribution of fracture patterns in immature (blue)
and mature (orange) pelvic groups. Note the increased percentage of ramus and iliac wing
fractures in the immature group and the increased percentage of acetabular and diastasis

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The mechanism of injury is important to determine because high-energy injuries may result in
polytrauma. The most common mechanisms of injury include motor vehicle collisions, a
pedestrian or bicyclist struck by a motor vehicle, and a fall from a substantial height.
Avulsion injuries may result from a minor fall or twisting injury sustained while kicking a ball or
jumping, among other activities.
Physical Examination
An initial full trauma evaluation should be performed, including airway, breathing, and
circulatory assessment.30
Evaluation of the head, chest, abdomen, spine, and pelvic region should be performed.
Complete examination includes evaluation of the scrotum/vagina, urethra, and rectum to
identify open injury or coexisting injury.
Consider a retrograde urethrogram before catheterization if urethral injury is suspected.
Open pelvic ring fractures in pediatric patients are associated with a high rate of
complications.31
Inspect the skin for Morel-Lavallee lesions.
Shearing of subcutaneous fat and skin from the underlying fascia
Rare in young patients but can occur in older, adolescent patients with obesity who sustain
pelvic injuries.
Assess hip range of motion, leg lengths, and extremity positioning to evaluate for hip
dislocation.
In posterior dislocations, the hip usually is held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation.
In anterior dislocations, the hip usually is held in extension, abduction, and external rotation.
In inferior dislocations, the hip usually is flexed and adducted, possibly lying on the
abdomen. The knee also usually is flexed in this position.

Nonsurgical Management
Most pelvic ring fractures and avulsions in children are managed nonsurgically.
Depending on fracture type and severity, treatment options include bed rest, bed-to-chair
transfers, and protected–weight bearing with the use of a walker or crutches for 3 to 4 weeks,
followed by progressive–weight bearing. Some fractures may require protection and
immobilization with the use of a spica cast.
Indications
Type I fractures (pelvic avulsion fractures).
Type II fractures (iliac wing fractures) are managed via protected–weight bearing or activity
limitations alone, depending on patient comfort, for 3 to 4 weeks, followed by gradual return
to normal activities.
Type III fractures (ring fractures without segmental instability)—Because most of these fracture
patterns are stable, nonsurgical treatment is indicated in most patients. Management typically
consists of pain control and progressive–weight bearing as tolerated (with the use of crutches
or a walker if necessary) for 4 to 6 weeks, followed by gradual return to activities.
If these injuries involve the acetabulum, initial non–weight bearing is recommended,
followed by progressive advancement to weight bearing as tolerated.
A spica cast can be used in patients with excessive discomfort or patients who may not be
able to abide by activity restrictions.
Careful monitoring of hemodynamic status is required in patients with a type IIIB fracture
pattern because of an increased risk of blood loss.
Type IV fractures (ring disruptions with segmental instability)—These fracture types are
associated with less than 2 cm of displacement and may be managed nonsurgically; a trend
toward surgical management recently has been observed.
Initial management consists of pain control and bed rest for 3 to 4 weeks, followed by
protected–weight bearing for an additional 3 to 4 weeks, depending on the fracture pattern.

The goals of the surgical management of unstable pelvic ring fractures include the following:
Stabilization of unstable fracture patterns
Anatomic restoration of anatomy to decrease the risks of osteoarthritis of the hips and

Early mobilization, especially for polytrauma patients

Pelvic asymmetry greater than 1 cm35

Anterior and posterior ring disruption

Displaced iliac wing fractures that extend into the sacroiliac joint (crescent fracture)

Wound care for open fractures
Control hemorrhage during resuscitation
Allow for earlier mobilization
Easier nursing care/patient comfort

Outcomes
Most pediatric pelvis fractures result in no long-term complications.
Mortality from pelvic fractures and related hemorrhage occurs in less than 1% of patients,
which is much lower than the rate in adults. Most deaths in pediatric patients with a pelvic ring
injury can be attributed to neurologic or visceral injuries.
Rates of mortality, genitourinary injury, other musculoskeletal injury, transfusion, and
laparotomy are increased with higher fracture classification.
